walkthroughs.body_html:
Genes & Health — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Genes & Health brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Genes & Health.

mcqs.q: What does a gene code for?
options: ADH directly opens holes in the collecting duct that let urine escape.
A gene codes for a specific physical feature like eye colour directly.
Typically a polypeptide (protein) — through transcription to mRNA and translation by ribosomes.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.

mcqs.q: How does ADH affect the collecting duct in the kidney?
options: ADH directly opens holes in the collecting duct that let urine escape.
It increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water (by inserting aquaporins), so more water is reabsorbed and urine is more concentrated.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
ADH actively pumps water out of urine into the blood.

mcqs.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker muscular wall than the right?
options: The left ventricle is thicker because it handles oxygenated blood, which is harder to pump.
It must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body; the right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs.
ADH directly opens holes in the collecting duct that let urine escape.
The left ventricle is thicker because it is on the same side as the brain.
